  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Psychiatrist
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Avoid Sex: Sex, Avoid Sleep: Going to sleep or lying in the dark
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
The Tuesday afternoon rain had made the highway glassy when Aroha’s vehicle was struck. She could not yet place which impact came first—the rear-end jolt or the side-door crush—or whether the airbags had deployed before the glass gave way. At fifty-eight, she still could not tell a clear story of what happened even to herself, let alone to her patients. The sequence of the accident remained tangled, a knot of metal and motion that refused to untie into a linear account. In the weeks that followed, Aroha felt jumpy, her shoulders tightening at the sudden clatter of a falling pen or the brake of a passing car. At home, she felt unsafe unless her back was against a wall where she could see the room. Each night, she woke during the night to check whether she was safe, fully alert, listening for the phantom screech of tires, convinced the threat was still present. The world outside her window, once ordinary, now felt dangerously unpredictable. A passing truck, a sudden turn, or the sight of a delivery van reversing at a curb could instantly bring back the full memory without warning. The crash imagery of cars hit by accident would surface, vivid and unbidden, pulling the event out of the past and into the room. Aroha tried to tell the story of the crash, but she could not tell a clear story of what happened even to herself. The memories did not line up. She could not put the memories of the event in the right order, the impacts and the sounds overlapping in her mind like overlapping photographs. Unwanted thoughts drifted through her awareness, persistent and sharp, arriving without any clear signal. Aroha worked as a psychiatrist at a bustling downtown clinic. She sat in her office chair with her spine aligned to the bookshelf, avoiding the open windows that let in too much street noise. She tried hard to control her emotions, her hands resting quietly on her desk, her voice steady as she reviewed case files. The days passed, and her avoidance deepened. She declined evening gatherings with former colleagues, finding the low lighting and close quarters uncomfortable. Over months, she avoided sex, the physical closeness and the vulnerability of the dark feeling like exposure. Her divorce settled into quiet finality, the two lives moving apart without conflict. At her desk, a trauma-related event could arrive without warning; a sudden honk or a car merging too closely would catch her attention, her gaze fixed on the flow of vehicles, certain that the world was a dangerous place, littered with hidden threats that could catch her off guard. She had come to believe she was permanently changed for the worse, her nervous system forever set to high alert, her mind a place where the past and present coexisted. Aroha could not trust that she would do the right thing when the pressure mounted, whether she was prescribing a medication or simply crossing a busy street. The habits of avoidance and threat monitoring settled into her routine. She avoided sleep, going to sleep or lying in the dark, her back still braced against the wall. She avoided sex, keeping her body separate. She maintained her composure, controlling her emotions. The symptoms did not drive one another; they simply occupied her days, each one present and real. Now, the weight of these habits has finally brought Aroha back to therapy. She lies awake in her bedroom, her eyes fixed on the darkened ceiling, wondering if the quiet of the night is truly safe or merely a pause before the next impact. She is afraid of losing her hard-won control, of slipping into the same helplessness she felt in the wreck, but she is also hoping, quietly, to make sense of the accident, to trust her own mind again, and to sleep without checking the dark.
